children: U.S. banks hold roughly $3.09 trillion in commercial real estate (CRE) debt, but that debt is far from evenly spread out. Smaller regional and community lenders, a banking sub-sector that commands only about 13.5% of assets, are carrying nearly two-thirds of CRE exposure.

At a glance, the situation looks outstanding, like the 2008 crash never happened. FDIC Call Report filings show regional bank CRE delinquency rates around 0.73% and 1.25%. However, the commercial mortgage-backed security (CMBS) market says otherwise.

In September 2026, the CMBS delinquency rate surged to 8.02% – the highest since November 2020. Meanwhile, the rate measuring transfers due to default, imminent default, or other distress – aka the special servicing rate- hit a 13-year high of 11.49%
Trepp’s

newest data shows that even as a single $975 million showroom loan cure pulled the headline rate to 7.87%, stress deepened across every major property type. Office climbed 17 basis points to 12.33%, multifamily rose to 8.09%, and retail jumped 63 basis points to 7.21%.

Regional bank books aren’t outperforming the securitized market through superior underwriting, but rather by using discretionary accounting and extend-and-pretend modifications. These banks mask underwater maturities that CMBS trusts are legally forced to expose.
The Accounting Loophole Hiding the Damage

Under ASU 2022-02, banks must report loan modifications only when they determine a borrower is experiencing "financial difficulty." The issue, however, is that the banks themselves make the call. Thus, an underwater borrower can receive a balloon-payment extension classified as a routine renewal, avoiding troubled-debt classification.

The scale of the omission is striking. A year ago, the St. Louis Fed showed banks officially reported just $27.7 billion in modified CRE loans for borrowers in financial difficulty—less than 1% of the $3 trillion-plus market.
Yet, Federal Reserve Board research by
David Glancy
and NY Fed supervisory data from
Crosignani
and
Prazad

reveal that large banks actually extended roughly half of all maturing CRE loans. The discrepancy confirms massive unreported evergreening by weakly capitalized lenders protecting their regulatory capital cushions.
The concentration risk is structural. Research by
Columbia, Wharton,
and
MIT

finds 53% of U.S. regional banks already exceed the 300% CRE-to-capital regulatory threshold, with a median concentration of 310%. Commercial mortgages represent 38% of total assets at a typical regional bank versus just 8% at money-center banks.
The Problem With A Bearish Bet

The bear thesis treats the public CMBS market as a mirror for regional bank loan books, while securitized trusts disproportionately hold the highest-leverage, non-recourse transitional debt. Meanwhile, bank-held multifamily delinquencies were as low as 1.4% in Q2, and Freddie Mac’s $500 billion-plus apartment portfolio remains below 0.8%.
These dynamics make broad short bets against vehicles like the
SPDR S&P Regional Banking ETF

Q3 earnings from operators like

and

, with the former lifting reserve coverage to 118% and growing EPS 7.5% to $2.45. Meanwhile, the latter posted a 20% EPS jump to $1.78.
East West Bancorp
delivered record third-quarter revenue and EPS of $2.76 with nonperforming assets at a pristine 0.30% of total assets and a CET1 ratio above 15%, while
Banc of California
—having already offloaded $827 million in commercial real estate and construction loans during the second quarter—rebounded with a 21% EPS gain and wider lending margins.

The final hurdle to shorting is the consolidation trend. M&A has been ongoing in the sector since the 1990s. According to Marketplace, since 1986, the number of banks has decreased from around 18,000 to just over 4,200. Thus, if a distressed bank has specific value to a buyer, it can be acquired at a premium, lowering the shorting appeal.

title: Why the $3 Trillion ‘Extend and Pretend’ Bank Short Is a Trap
